reference.source: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery / Sabiston Textbook of Surgery
clinicalPearls: Hepatic hydatid disease is caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, with dogs as definitive hosts and humans as accidental intermediate hosts, and is endemic in sheep- and cattle-rearing regions
The liver is the commonest organ affected, and cysts are frequently asymptomatic for years, presenting as a slowly enlarging right upper quadrant mass or dull ache
Ultrasound and CT show a characteristic cyst with a wall, internal daughter cysts, and detached membranes; the Gharbi/WHO classification helps stage activity
Serology supports the diagnosis, though false negatives occur, and eosinophilia may be present
Diagnostic aspiration is traditionally avoided because of the risk of spillage causing anaphylaxis and peritoneal seeding, although image-guided PAIR is used in selected cases under cover

Management options include the PAIR technique (puncture, aspiration, injection of a scolicidal agent, and re-aspiration), surgery, and anthelmintic therapy, chosen by cyst stage, size, and complications
Perioperative and periprocedural anthelmintic cover and meticulous protection of the field with scolicidal precautions reduce recurrence and spillage
reference.pathophysiology: Humans acquire infection by ingesting Echinococcus eggs shed in canine faeces. Embryos penetrate the intestinal wall and travel via the portal circulation, with the liver acting as the first filter and commonest site of lodgement. There the larva develops into a fluid-filled hydatid cyst with three layers: an outer host-derived fibrous pericyst, a middle acellular laminated membrane, and an inner germinal layer that produces protoscolices and daughter cysts. The cyst enlarges slowly and can compress adjacent liver, bile ducts, and vessels. Cyst fluid is highly antigenic, so rupture, whether spontaneous, traumatic, or iatrogenic, can release protoscolices that seed new cysts and trigger a severe allergic or anaphylactic reaction. Communication with the biliary tree can cause cholangitis and obstructive jaundice.
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound to characterise and stage the cyst
CT or MRI for anatomical detail, biliary communication, and surgical planning
Echinococcal serology (with awareness of false negatives)
MRCP or ERCP when biliary communication or obstruction is suspected
Chest imaging to exclude concurrent pulmonary hydatid disease
redFlags: Cyst rupture provoking anaphylaxis or anaphylactic shock, a life-threatening emergency
Rupture or communication into the biliary tree causing cholangitis and obstructive jaundice
Secondary bacterial infection of the cyst with sepsis
Rupture into the peritoneum or thorax with widespread secondary seeding
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally good for uncomplicated cysts treated appropriately, with high cure rates after surgery or PAIR combined with anthelmintic therapy. Recurrence can occur from spillage of viable protoscolices, and prognosis is worse with complications such as anaphylaxis, biliary rupture, or secondary infection.
pitfalls: Aspirating or biopsying an undiagnosed cyst and precipitating spillage, seeding, or anaphylaxis
Omitting perioperative anthelmintic cover and scolicidal precautions, increasing recurrence
Injecting a scolicidal agent when there is biliary communication, risking sclerosing cholangitis
Mistaking a hydatid cyst for a simple cyst or abscess and managing it inappropriately
